column1: # Which released kan each day commit works with (day#94).
# Measured by .github/workflows/kan-compat.yml: one cell per kan tag, running
# tests/kan_conformance.rs — the only suite in this repo that talks to a real
# kan rather than a DAY_KAN_BIN stub.
# The cell SKIPS `conformance_kan_78_*`, which asserts a property of kan rather
# than a dependency of day. Including it made this table wrong by one release:
# day emits `kan result` with its subject positionally and never with
# `--subject`, so a kan predating kan#78 serves day fine. Only tests of day's
# own dependencies may set the floor.
# src/compat.rs's OLDEST_SUPPORTED and NEWEST_MEASURED are DERIVED from the
# `ok` rows here, and tests/kan_compat.rs fails if they drift apart. Do not
# edit one without the other.
# Outcomes:
#   ok            every conformance test passed
#   incompatible  at least one failed — day depends on something absent
#   unbuildable   the tag does not build with the current toolchain; says
#                 nothing about the pairing
# A tag with no row here is WARNED about, not failed. Whether a pairing is
# supported is still a decision rather than a default — but the decision is
# expressed by the range being derived only from the rows that are present, so
# an unmeasured kan leaves day's claim true and its user gets the `Newer`
# verdict, which is the designed benign path.
# This line used to say "fails the build", which stopped being true when the
# workflow was changed to warn: kan publishing a tag would otherwise turn DAY's
# next release red, after the tag was already pushed, for an expected event in
# another repo. Stale operative guidance in the file a maintainer edits to
# adopt a version, found by a cold review.
# The floor is HARD, not incidental. Since day#71, `ClaimLog` makes exactly one
# `kan show --all --json` call, so a kan without that flag cannot answer a
# single claim probe. day does not fall back, deliberately: a fallback is a
# two-mode mechanism, and this repo's record says that is where defects hide
# (day#91, and twice in v0.7.0-beta.3 alone).
# NOTE: `show --all` landed in v0.9.1, NOT v0.9.0 — v0.9.0 has an `--all` flag
# on `publish`, which is what a substring grep finds and what the measurement
# correctly refused to believe.
